mainTopic: How רבי מאיר's view of 'מכלל לאו אתה שומע הן' is resolved, and the new משנה on שבועת הפקדון: who is liable, how many קרבנות, and the rule that a קנס brings no liability
overview: The amud opens by finishing the question of whether רבי מאיר accepts the rule 'מכלל לאו אתה שומע הן', inferring a positive from a negative. The גמרא first reverses the opinions in the משנה and says רבי מאיר rejects the rule even in איסור. רבינא attacks this from the drunk and long-haired כהנים, whose death penalty is learned exactly this way. The final answer keeps the reversal: רבי מאיר rejects the rule only in money matters, and סוטה counts as an איסור that involves money. After the הדרן for פרק שבועת העדות, a new משנה begins about שבועת הפקדון, a false oath denying someone's money or property. It explains who is bound by this oath, the argument between רבי מאיר and חכמים about needing a בית דין, which states of mind bring an אשם, and how many קרבנות are owed for repeated oaths, several claimants, or several items. It ends with cases of a קנס and the general rule: a person is liable only if his own admission would have made him pay. The גמרא then opens with a story about three students in רבה's study hall, and רב כהנא's question continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Reverse the opinions: רבי מאיר rejects the rule even in איסור
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא proposes switching the opinions in the משנה, so that רבי מאיר exempts the witnesses. It adds that רבי מאיר does not accept 'מכלל לאו אתה שומע הן' even in matters of איסור.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, reverse the opinions. רבי מאיר does not accept the rule even in איסור matters.
steps.whatsHappening: After the money-versus-איסור split ran into trouble from סוטה, the גמרא tries a new approach. It swaps the opinions in the משנה and says רבי מאיר never infers a positive from a negative, not even in איסור.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once the opinions are reversed, רבי מאיר exempts the witnesses in our משנה, which fits his known view. The problem of סוטה also goes away, because now רבי מאיר rejects the rule everywhere. But this is a sweeping claim, and the next step will test it.

keyTerms.meaning: Reverse, meaning switch which תנא holds which opinion
Ritual or prohibition matters, as opposed to money
He does not hold of (this principle)
From a negative statement you can infer the positive

phrases.english: Rather, reverse it:
phrases.notes: Switch the names in the משנה, so now רבי מאיר is the one who exempts the witnesses.

phrases.english: even in ritual matters he does not accept it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אֵיפוֹךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the earlier rejected money-versus-איסור distinction with a new approach.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reattribution of opinions plus a broad claim about רבי מאיר's method
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי מאיר accepts the rule in איסור but not in money, yet סוטה seemed to contradict that.
steps.terutzMaskana: Reverse the משנה; רבי מאיר rejects the rule in all areas, even איסור.

steps.title: רבינא challenges: the drunk and long-haired כהנים are liable to death
steps.stepSummary: רבינא asks how רבי מאיר could reject the rule in איסור. The death penalty for a כהן who serves drunk or with overgrown hair is itself learned from a negative statement, and a משנה lists it without any dispute.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא objected: Does he really not accept it in איסור? If so, the drunk and long-haired כהנים, who are liable to death, should not be liable according to רבי מאיר! But we learned: These are liable to death: those drunk on wine and those with overgrown hair.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא attacks the claim from Step 1 that רבי מאיר rejects the rule even in איסור. He points to a well-known halacha that depends on exactly this kind of inference.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The death penalty for the drunk כהן comes from a פסוק that says 'do not drink wine… so that you will not die'. From that negative wording we infer that if he does drink and serve, he will die. If רבי מאיר never made such inferences, he would have to disagree with that הלכה. Yet the משנה states it with no dissent.

keyTerms.meaning: He objected to it, a strong challenge
כהנים who serve after drinking wine
כהנים who serve with overgrown, uncut hair
Death at the hands of Heaven

steps.confusionAlert: רבינא is not arguing about סוטה or witnesses here. He is only attacking the broad claim that רבי מאיר rejects the rule in איסור too.

phrases.english: Ravina objected to it:
And in ritual matters he does not accept it?!
But if so,
those drunk on wine and those with overgrown hair, who are liable to death,

phrases.aramaic: הָכִי נָמֵי דְּלֵית לֵיהּ לְרַבִּי מֵאִיר?!
phrases.english: would רבי מאיר also not hold of this?!
But didn't we learn:

phrases.aramaic: אֵלּוּ שֶׁבְּמִיתָה – שְׁתוּיֵי יַיִן וּפְרוּעֵי רֹאשׁ!
phrases.english: These are the ones liable to death: those drunk on wine and those with overgrown hair!

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְקֵיף לֵיהּ רָבִינָא: וּבְאִיסּוּרָא לֵית לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Directly attacks the claim in Step 1 that רבי מאיר rejects the rule even in איסור.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that רבי מאיר does not accept 'מכלל לאו אתה שומע הן' even in איסור.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The death penalty for drunk or long-haired כהנים rests on inferring a positive from a negative. It appears in a משנה with no dissent, so רבי מאיר must accept the rule at least in איסור.

steps.title: Final answer: reverse the opinions; רבי מאיר rejects the rule only in money, and סוטה involves money
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא keeps the reversal of the opinions but limits it. רבי מאיר rejects the rule only in money matters and accepts it in איסור. סוטה is different because it is an איסור that also involves money.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, really reverse the opinions. When he does not accept the rule, that is in money matters; in איסור matters he accepts it. And סוטה is different, because it is an איסור that has money in it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives its final answer. It keeps the reversal from Step 1 but drops the claim that רבי מאיר rejects the rule in איסור.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since רבי מאיר accepts the rule in איסור, the drunk and long-haired כהנים are no problem. סוטה, which earlier seemed to show him rejecting the rule in איסור, is explained as an איסור that carries money consequences, like whether she loses her כתובה. So there he treats it like a money case. Our case of שבועת העדות also has a money side, so after the reversal רבי מאיר exempts the witnesses.

keyTerms.meaning: Actually, really (going back to an earlier idea)
A wife suspected of adultery who goes through the bitter-water process

steps.whatToRemember: Final view: reverse the משנה. רבי מאיר does not apply 'מכלל לאו אתה שומע הן' to money matters, but does apply it to איסור. An איסור that involves money, like סוטה, counts as money for this purpose.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that a case can belong to the category of איסור while still being handled like money, because of its money side.

phrases.english: Rather, actually reverse it;
when he does not accept it, that is in money matters;
in ritual matters he does accept it;
and סוטה is different,
because it is a ritual matter that has money in it.
phrases.notes: Money here means things like her כתובה, which depends on the outcome.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא לְעוֹלָם תֵּיפוֹךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבינא's challenge by narrowing Step 1: the reversal stays, but רבי מאיר accepts the rule in איסור.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the principle plus distinguishing a mixed case
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי מאיר rejects the rule everywhere, even in איסור.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי מאיר rejects the rule only in money. סוטה, and our שבועת העדות case, are איסור matters with money involved, so he rejects it there too.

steps.title: Hadran — Closing פרק שבועת העדות
steps.stepSummary: The closing formula marking the end of the פרק on שבועת העדות.
steps.simpleTranslation: We will return to you, שבועת העדות.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the traditional line said when finishing a פרק. It closes the פרק of שבועת העדות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The הדרן is not part of the argument. It marks that the discussion of the witness oath is complete and that a new topic, the oath about a deposit, comes next.

keyTerms.meaning: We will return to you, said at the end of a פרק
The oath of testimony, the name of this פרק

phrases.english: We will return to you, Shevuat HaEdut

steps.triggerLanguage: הֲדַרַן עֲלָךְ שְׁבוּעַת הָעֵדוּת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Formally closes the פרק after the final resolution in Step 3.

steps.title: The deposit oath applies to everyone
steps.stepSummary: The new משנה opens by saying that שבועת הפקדון applies to men and women, to relatives and non-relatives, and to people who are fit or unfit to testify.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: The oath about a deposit applies to men and to women, to people who are not related and to relatives, and to people who are fit to testify and to people who are not.
steps.whatsHappening: A new פרק begins with a new משנה about שבועת הפקדון. It first tells us who this oath applies to: basically everyone.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the last פרק, שבועת העדות applied only to people fit to be witnesses. Here there is no such limit, because this oath is about denying money you hold, not about testifying. So relatives and people unfit to testify are included too.

keyTerms.meaning: Our משנה. It marks the start of the משנה text.
The oath about a deposit: falsely swearing that you do not hold someone's money or object.
People unfit to serve as witnesses

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the whole new פרק and shows right away how שבועת הפקדון is different from שבועת העדות.

phrases.english: MISHNA: The oath about a deposit
applies to men and to women
to people who are not related and to relatives
to those fit to testify and to those unfit

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִי׳ שְׁבוּעַת הַפִּקָּדוֹן נוֹהֶגֶת בַּאֲנָשִׁים וּבְנָשִׁים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new פרק right after the closing formula of the פרק on שבועת העדות.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: שבועת הפקדון applies to all people, with no limits based on gender, being related, or being fit to testify.

steps.title: רבי מאיר: an oath imposed by others counts only in court
steps.stepSummary: If a person swears on his own, he is liable whether or not he is in front of a court. According to רבי מאיר, if someone else made him swear, he is liable only if he denied it in בית דין.
steps.simpleTranslation: Whether in front of a court or not in front of a court, he is liable if he swore on his own. But if others made him swear, he is not liable until he denies it in court. These are the words of רבי מאיר.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה now deals with where the oath has to be taken. רבי מאיר splits it into two cases: an oath he said by himself, and an oath someone else put on him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If he swears by himself, it does not matter where he is. If someone else makes him swear, for example by saying 'I make you swear' and he answers 'אמן', רבי מאיר says that counts only when he denies the claim in בית דין.

keyTerms.meaning: From his own mouth: he says the oath himself.
From others' mouths: someone else puts the oath on him.
That he denies it, saying the claim is false.

steps.confusionAlert: The phrase 'in front of a court and not in front of a court' belongs to the case of swearing 'on his own'. Only the oath others put on him needs a court, according to רבי מאיר.

phrases.aramaic: בִּפְנֵי בֵּית דִּין וְשֶׁלֹּא בִּפְנֵי בֵּית דִּין
phrases.english: in front of a court and not in front of a court
when he swore on his own
but when others made him swear

phrases.aramaic: אֵינוֹ חַיָּיב עַד שֶׁיִּכְפְּרֶנּוּ בְּבֵית דִּין
phrases.english: he is not liable until he denies it in court
these are the words of Rabbi Meir

steps.triggerLanguage: בִּפְנֵי בֵּית דִּין וְשֶׁלֹּא בִּפְנֵי בֵּית דִּין מִפִּי עַצְמוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the משנה, moving from who the oath applies to over to where and how it must be taken.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבי מאיר, an oath he says himself makes him liable anywhere. An oath others put on him makes him liable only if he denies the claim in בית דין.

steps.title: The Sages: once he denied, he is liable
steps.stepSummary: חכמים disagree with רבי מאיר. Whether he swore on his own or others made him swear, he is liable as soon as he falsely denied the claim, even outside a court.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the Sages say: whether he swore on his own or others made him swear, once he denied it, he is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: חכמים argue with רבי מאיר's split between the two cases. For them, a court is never needed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי מאיר requires בית דין when others put the oath on him. חכמים say what matters is the false denial itself. So both kinds of oath make him liable anywhere.

keyTerms.meaning: The Sages, the majority opinion arguing with רבי מאיר

steps.whatToRemember: רבי מאיר: an oath others put on him counts only in בית דין. חכמים: any false denial under oath counts, in court or not.

phrases.english: And the Sages say

phrases.aramaic: בֵּין מִפִּי עַצְמוֹ בֵּין מִפִּי אֲחֵרִים
phrases.english: whether he swore on his own or others made him swear
once he denied it, he is liable

steps.triggerLanguage: וַחֲכָמִים אוֹמְרִים בֵּין מִפִּי עַצְמוֹ בֵּין מִפִּי אֲחֵרִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the opinion that argues with רבי מאיר's ruling in the previous step.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to חכמים, a false denial under oath makes him liable whether he swore himself or others made him swear, even outside בית דין.

steps.title: Which mistakes count, and the guilt offering
steps.stepSummary: He is liable for a deliberate false oath. He is also liable when he knew he was keeping the deposit but did not know the oath brings a קרבן. He is not liable when the whole thing was an honest mistake. The קרבן is an אשם worth silver shekels.
steps.simpleTranslation: And he is liable for a deliberate false oath, and for an oath sworn by mistake together with deliberately keeping the deposit. But he is not liable for a mistaken oath alone. And what is he liable for when it is deliberate? A guilt offering worth silver shekels.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה explains which states of mind make a person liable for שבועת הפקדון. Then it says what he brings: an אשם.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Usually a קרבן is brought only for a mistake. Here it is brought even for a deliberate lie. It is also brought when he knew the money was not his but did not know the oath brings a קרבן. If he honestly thought he owed nothing, he brings nothing. The אשם must be worth silver shekels.

keyTerms.meaning: Silver shekels: the value the אשם must reach

steps.confusionAlert: Do not assume a קרבן is only for mistakes. For שבועת הפקדון the אשם is brought even when he lied on purpose.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the basic rule for when a false deposit oath requires an אשם. The rest of the פרק builds on it.

phrases.english: And he is liable for swearing the false oath on purpose
and for a mistaken oath together with keeping the deposit on purpose
phrases.notes: He knew he was lying about the deposit. He just didn't know that this kind of oath brings a קרבן.

phrases.english: but he is not liable for a mistaken oath alone
And what is he liable for when he swore on purpose?
a guilt offering worth silver shekels
phrases.notes: 'Shekels' is plural, so the animal must be worth at least two shekels.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְחַיָּיב עַל זְדוֹן הַשְּׁבוּעָה וְעַל שִׁגְגָתָהּ עִם זְדוֹן הַפִּקָּדוֹן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The argument about the court is finished. The משנה now moves on to state of mind and the type of קרבן.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: He brings an אשם worth silver shekels for a deliberate false deposit oath, or for knowingly keeping the deposit without knowing the oath brings a קרבן. He brings nothing for an honest mistake alone.

steps.title: How the oath of deposit happens
steps.stepSummary: The משנה gives two ways a שבועת הפקדון can happen: the defendant swears on his own, or the claimant makes him swear and he answers אמן.
steps.simpleTranslation: How does a שבועת הפקדון work? The claimant says, 'Give me my deposit that you are holding,' and the defendant answers, 'I swear you have nothing with me.' Or the defendant says, 'You have nothing with me,' the claimant says, 'I make you swear,' and the defendant says 'אמן.' In both cases he is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה explains what a שבועת הפקדון looks like in real life. It gives two examples.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first case the defendant swears by himself. In the second case the claimant gives the oath and the defendant accepts it by saying אמן. Answering אמן counts just like saying the oath himself, so he is liable either way.

keyTerms.meaning: How? A משנה uses this to open a detailed explanation.
A deposit, something left with another person for safekeeping.
I make you swear. The claimant gives the oath to the defendant.
Amen. Saying it accepts the oath as if he swore it himself.

steps.confusionAlert: Even though the defendant never says the word 'oath' in the second case, his אמן makes it a full oath and he is liable.

phrases.english: How does the oath of deposit work?
He said to him: Give me my deposit
that I have in your possession
and he answered: I swear you have nothing in my possession
or he said to him: You have nothing in my possession
and the claimant said: I make you swear
and he said 'Amen'; he is liable.

steps.triggerLanguage: שְׁבוּעַת הַפִּקָּדוֹן כֵּיצַד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the general rules about who is liable to a concrete description of how the oath happens.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A false denial of a deposit is a liable oath whether he swears himself or answers אמן to the claimant's oath.

steps.title: Five oaths bring five liabilities
steps.stepSummary: If the claimant made him swear five times and he falsely denied each time, he owes a קרבן for every single oath.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the claimant made him swear five times, in front of a בית דין or not, and he denied each time, he is liable for each one.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה now asks what happens when the same oath is repeated five times. It rules that each false oath counts on its own.
steps.deeperAnalysis: You might think that once he has already denied the deposit under oath, more oaths add nothing. The משנה says no: each new oath is a new false denial and needs its own קרבן. This holds even outside a בית דין.

keyTerms.meaning: He denied, meaning he falsely said he did not have the item.
For each and every one, so each oath is counted separately.

phrases.english: If he made him swear five times,
whether in front of a court
or not in front of a court,

phrases.aramaic: וְכָפַר – חַיָּיב עַל כׇּל אַחַת וְאַחַת.
phrases.english: and he denied, he is liable for each and every one.

steps.triggerLanguage: הִשְׁבִּיעַ עָלָיו חָמֵשׁ פְּעָמִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After defining one oath, the משנה asks about the same oath repeated several times.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Each repeated false oath of deposit brings its own קרבן, in or out of court.

steps.title: רבי שמעון explains why each oath counts
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמעון explains that each oath counts because after every oath the defendant could have changed his mind and admitted the truth.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמעון said: What is the reason? Because he could have gone back and admitted.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי שמעון gives the reason for the rule in the last step. He explains why five oaths mean five liabilities.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Between one oath and the next, the defendant had a real chance to admit and pay back. When he chose to swear falsely again instead, he made a new false denial. That is why every oath counts separately.

keyTerms.meaning: To go back and admit the truth.

phrases.english: Rabbi Shimon said: What is the reason?
Because he is able to go back and admit.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן: מָה טַעַם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the reason behind the ruling of five liabilities.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Each oath is a new denial because he could have admitted in between.

steps.title: Five claimants: one general oath or separate denials
steps.stepSummary: If five people sue him together and he swears once to all of them, he owes one קרבן. If he denies each one separately, he owes for each.
steps.simpleTranslation: If five people were suing him and said, 'Give us our deposit that you are holding,' and he said, 'I swear none of you have anything with me,' he is liable only once. If he said, 'I swear you have nothing with me, and not you, and not you,' he is liable for each one.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה now looks at several claimants instead of several oaths. It explains when the oath counts once and when it counts for each person.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One sentence to the whole group ('none of you') is one oath, so there is one קרבן. When he points to each person ('not you, and not you'), he has denied each claim on its own, so he owes for each one.

keyTerms.meaning: To all of you, said to the whole group at once.

steps.confusionAlert: The amount of money or the number of people does not decide the count. What matters is how he worded the denial: one general sentence, or separate denials for each person.

phrases.english: If five people were suing him
and they said to him: Give us the deposit
that we have in your possession
and he said: I swear none of you have anything in my possession
he is liable only once.
But if he said: I swear you have nothing in my possession,
and not you, and not you
phrases.notes: He is turning to each claimant one by one.

phrases.english: he is liable for each and every one.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָיוּ חֲמִשָּׁה תּוֹבְעִים אוֹתוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from one claimant with many oaths to many claimants at once.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A general oath to a group brings one קרבן; separate denials to each claimant bring a קרבן for each.

steps.title: How clearly must the word 'oath' be said?
steps.stepSummary: רבי אליעזר says he is liable for each claimant only if he says 'oath' at the end. רבי שמעון says he must say 'oath' to each and every claimant.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אליעזר says: only if he says 'oath' at the end. רבי שמעון says: only if he says 'oath' to each and every one.
steps.whatsHappening: Two תנאים disagree with the last ruling about separate denials. They ask whether one word 'oath' at the start is enough to cover every person.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ruling we just saw says one 'oath' at the beginning followed by 'not you, and not you' is enough. רבי אליעזר wants the word 'oath' repeated at the end too, so it clearly covers each denial. רבי שמעון is strictest: the word 'oath' must be said separately to each claimant.

keyTerms.meaning: Not unless he says. Sets a requirement for being liable.

steps.whatToRemember: There are three views on separate liability for several claimants: the first opinion needs one 'oath' at the start, רבי אליעזר needs 'oath' at the end too, and רבי שמעון needs 'oath' for each person.

phrases.english: Rabbi Eliezer says:
Not unless he says 'oath' at the end.
Rabbi Shimon says:

phrases.aramaic: עַד שֶׁיֹּאמַר שְׁבוּעָה לְכׇל אֶחָד וְאֶחָד.
phrases.english: Not unless he says 'oath' to each and every one.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר אוֹמֵר: עַד שֶׁיֹּאמַר שְׁבוּעָה בָּאַחֲרוֹנָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disputes the wording needed for the separate liability ruled in the previous step.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי אליעזר: 'oath' must also come at the end; רבי שמעון: 'oath' must be said to each claimant.

steps.title: Several kinds of items: one denial or many
steps.stepSummary: If one claimant demands a deposit, a loan pledge, a stolen item, and a lost item, a general denial counts once. Naming each item in the oath counts for each.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he said, 'Give me the deposit, the pledge, the stolen item, and the lost item that you are holding,' and the defendant said, 'I swear you have nothing with me,' he is liable only once. If he said, 'I swear I do not have your deposit, pledge, stolen item, or lost item,' he is liable for each one.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה uses the same idea for one claimant who demands several different kinds of things. Again, the wording of the oath decides the count.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A general 'you have nothing with me' is one denial covering everything, so there is one קרבן. When he names each type of item in his oath, he denies each claim separately, so he owes a קרבן for each.

keyTerms.meaning: Something handed over, such as money given as a loan or a partnership investment.
A lost item that he found.

steps.whatToRemember: In every case in this משנה the rule is the same: a single general denial counts once, while spelling out each person or each item makes every denial count separately.

phrases.english: Give me the deposit, and the item handed over,
the stolen item, and the lost item that I have in your possession
and he said: I swear you have nothing in my possession
he is liable only once.
But if he said: I swear you do not have in my possession
a deposit, an item handed over, a stolen item, or a lost item
he is liable for each and every one.

steps.triggerLanguage: תֵּן לִי פִּקָּדוֹן וּתְשׂוּמֶת יָד גָּזֵל וַאֲבֵידָה שֶׁיֵּשׁ לִי בְּיָדְךָ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the same rule about general versus separate denials to several items instead of several claimants.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A general denial of several items brings one קרבן; naming each item brings a קרבן for each.

steps.title: Wheat, barley and spelt: a general oath versus naming each item
steps.stepSummary: A general denial of wheat, barley and spelt counts as one oath. Naming each grain in the oath makes him liable for each one.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone says, "Give me the wheat, barley and spelt of mine that you are holding," and the other answers, "I swear you have nothing with me," he owes only one קרבן. If he answers, "I swear you have no wheat, barley or spelt with me," he owes a קרבן for each one.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives another example of the rule from step 14. This time the claim is about three kinds of grain.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The number of קרבנות depends on how the oath is worded, not on how many things were claimed. "You have nothing with me" is one denial. Naming wheat, barley and spelt separately makes three denials inside one oath.

phrases.english: "Give me the wheat, barley, and spelt
that I have in your possession";
"An oath that you have nothing in my possession":
he is liable only once.
"An oath that you do not have in my possession
wheat, barley, and spelt":
he is liable for each and every one.

steps.triggerLanguage: תֵּן לִי חִטִּין וּשְׂעוֹרִין וְכוּסְּמִין שֶׁיֵּשׁ לִי בְּיָדְךָ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another case applying the general-versus-specific oath rule from step 14.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A general denial counts as one oath. Naming each kind of grain counts as a separate oath for each.

steps.title: רבי מאיר: even single grains count separately
steps.stepSummary: רבי מאיר holds that even when the singular words are used, "a wheat, a barley, a spelt," he is liable for each one.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי מאיר says: even if he said "a wheat, a barley and a spelt," he owes a קרבן for each one.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי מאיר adds a further opinion to the grain case. He says the separate counting works even with this smaller wording.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The singular forms sound like tiny amounts, possibly just one grain of each. רבי מאיר still counts each named item as its own denial. He does not require each item to be a large amount.

keyTerms.meaning: A wheat, in the singular, sounding like one grain

phrases.english: Rabbi Meir says:
Even if he said "a wheat, a barley, and a spelt":
phrases.notes: These are the singular forms of the same three grains, so it sounds like he means just one grain of each.

phrases.english: he is liable for each and every one.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי מֵאִיר אוֹמֵר: אֲפִילּוּ אָמַר חִטָּה וּשְׂעוֹרָה וְכוּסֶּמֶת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Extends the grain case to the singular wording.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבי מאיר, even the singular wording makes him liable for each item.

steps.title: Falsely denying that he raped or seduced the daughter
steps.stepSummary: A father claims the man raped or seduced his daughter. The man denies it under oath. The first opinion says he is liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: The father says, "You raped or seduced my daughter." The man answers, "I did not rape and I did not seduce." The father says, "I make you swear," and the man says "Amen." He is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה starts a new topic: false oaths about payments that include a קנס, a fixed fine set by the תורה. Here the first opinion rules that he is liable.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A man who rapes or seduces a girl pays a fixed קנס. He also pays real money for her shame and for the damage to her value. The first opinion holds that his oath counts as denying money, so he is liable.

keyTerms.meaning: Amen; answering this accepts the oath as if he had said it himself

phrases.english: "You raped or seduced my daughter,"
and he says:
"I did not rape and I did not seduce";
"I make you swear,"
and he said "Amen": he is liable.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָנַסְתָּ וּפִיתִּיתָ אֶת בִּתִּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from counting oaths to whether denying a fine-related claim counts at all.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The first opinion: one who falsely swears he did not rape or seduce is liable.

steps.title: רבי שמעון exempts him because a fine is not paid by admission
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמעון disagrees and exempts him, since a person does not pay a קנס based on his own admission.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמעון says he is exempt, because a person does not pay a fine based on his own admission.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי שמעון argues with the first opinion about the rape and seduction case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A false oath is only serious if telling the truth would have made him pay. With a קנס, even if he had admitted, he would not have had to pay. So his denial did not take away any money from the father.

keyTerms.meaning: A fine set by the תורה, more than the actual loss

steps.whyThisMatters: The rule that a קנס is not paid by one's own admission is the key to every case in the rest of this section.

phrases.english: Rabbi Shimon exempts him,

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁאֵינוֹ מְשַׁלֵּם קְנָס עַל פִּי עַצְמוֹ.
phrases.english: since one does not pay a fine based on his own admission.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן פּוֹטֵר שֶׁאֵינוֹ מְשַׁלֵּם קְנָס עַל פִּי עַצְמוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with the ruling of step 17.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Denying a קנס under oath does not make one liable, since admitting it would not have made him pay.

steps.title: The חכמים answer: shame and damage are real money
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים reply that he still pays for shame and for damage based on his own admission, so his oath did deny money.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: Even though he does not pay the fine by his own admission, he does pay for shame and damage by his own admission.
steps.whatsHappening: The חכמים push back against רבי שמעון's reason. They defend the first opinion that he is liable.
steps.deeperAnalysis: They accept that the קנס is not paid by admission. But the claim also includes בושת and פגם, which are normal money payments. Since admitting would have made him pay those, his false oath took away real money.

keyTerms.meaning: Payment for the drop in her value

steps.whatToRemember: Everyone agrees a person is not liable for denying only a קנס. The argument here is whether the case also includes real money (בושת and פגם).

phrases.english: They said to him:

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵינוֹ מְשַׁלֵּם קְנָס עַל פִּי עַצְמוֹ,
phrases.english: Even though he does not pay a fine based on his own admission,

phrases.aramaic: מְשַׁלֵּם בּשֶׁת וּפְגָם עַל פִּי עַצְמוֹ.
phrases.english: he does pay for shame and damage based on his own admission.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרוּ לוֹ: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵינוֹ מְשַׁלֵּם קְנָס עַל פִּי עַצְמוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects רבי שמעון's reason and supports the ruling of step 17.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: His reason only covers the קנס, but the claim also includes money for shame and damage, which are paid by admission.

steps.title: Stolen ox: denying the theft versus denying the slaughter or sale
steps.stepSummary: Denying the theft under oath makes him liable. Admitting the theft but denying that he slaughtered or sold the ox makes him exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: "You stole my ox." He says, "I did not steal." "I make you swear," and he says "Amen": he is liable. If he says, "I stole it, but I did not slaughter or sell it," and the owner says "I make you swear," and he says "Amen": he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה applies the קנס rule to a thief. It sets two oaths about the same ox side by side.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Denying the theft denies the value of the ox itself, which is real money, so he is liable. Once he admits the theft, he is denying only the extra five-times payment for slaughtering or selling an ox. That extra payment is a קנס, so he is exempt.
steps.confusionAlert: In the second case he is still lying, and he still must return the ox. He is exempt only from the קרבן, because the part he denied is a קנס.

phrases.english: "You stole my ox,"
and he says, "I did not steal";
"I make you swear," and he said "Amen": he is liable.
"I stole, but I did not slaughter and I did not sell";
phrases.notes: A thief who slaughters or sells a stolen ox pays five times its value, as a fine.

phrases.english: "I make you swear," and he said "Amen": he is exempt.

steps.triggerLanguage: גָּנַבְתָּ אֶת שׁוֹרִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the rule that denying only a קנס does not make one liable.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Denying the theft makes him liable. Denying only the slaughter or sale (a קנס) makes him exempt.

steps.title: Ox that killed an ox versus ox that killed a slave
steps.stepSummary: Denying that his ox killed another's ox makes him liable. Denying that his ox killed a slave makes him exempt, because payment for a slave is a קנס.
steps.simpleTranslation: "Your ox killed my ox." He says, "It did not kill." "I make you swear," and he says "Amen": he is liable. "Your ox killed my slave." He says, "It did not kill." "I make you swear," and he says "Amen": he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives another pair of cases that show the difference between money and a קנס.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Payment for a killed ox is the ox's real value, so denying it denies money. Payment for a killed slave is a fixed thirty שקלים set by the תורה, which is a קנס. So the oath about the slave does not make him liable.
steps.whatToRemember: The test for a שבועת הפקדון: would telling the truth have made him pay money? If yes, he is liable. If the payment is only a קנס, he is exempt.

phrases.english: "Your ox killed my ox,"
and he says, "It did not kill";
"I make you swear," and he said "Amen": he is liable.
"Your ox killed my slave,"
phrases.notes: When an ox kills a slave, the owner pays a set thirty shekels no matter what the slave was worth, so it counts as a fine.

phrases.english: and he says, "It did not kill";
"I make you swear," and he said "Amen": he is exempt.

steps.triggerLanguage: הֵמִית שׁוֹרְךָ אֶת שׁוֹרִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A further application of the קנס rule, parallel to step 20.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Denying damage to an ox makes him liable. Denying the slave payment, which is a קנס, makes him exempt.

steps.title: Denying an injury under oath: liable
steps.stepSummary: A man says the other injured him and wounded him. The other denies it under oath. He is liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: One man says to another: "You hurt me and gave me a wound." The other answers: "I did not hurt you and I did not wound you." The first says: "I make you swear," and he answers "אמן." He is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives another case of a false oath: denying that you injured someone. Here the person who swore falsely is liable.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A person who injures a free person must pay for the damage, even if the only proof is his own admission. So his oath really did deny money he owed. That makes it a real שבועת הפקדון, and he is liable to bring the קרבן.

keyTerms.meaning: I make you swear (this is how the oath is placed on him)
Amen, which accepts the oath as if he said it himself
Liable (here: to bring a קרבן for the false oath)

phrases.english: He said to him: "You injured me
and you made a wound on me,"
and he says: "I did not injure you
and I did not make a wound on you";
"I make you swear," and he said "Amen": he is liable.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לוֹ: ״חָבַלְתָּ בִּי וְעָשִׂיתָ בִּי חַבּוּרָה״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the משנה's series of paired cases (liable or exempt), now with an injury to a free person.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Denying under oath that you injured someone makes you liable for the false oath, since injury payments are paid even based on your own admission.

steps.title: Denying knocking out a slave's tooth or eye: exempt
steps.stepSummary: A slave says his master knocked out his tooth and blinded his eye. The master denies it under oath. He is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: A slave says to his master: "You knocked out my tooth and blinded my eye." The master answers: "I did not knock it out and I did not blind it." The slave says: "I make you swear," and he answers "אמן." He is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives the opposite case: the master denies under oath an injury to his own slave, and he is exempt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When a master knocks out his slave's tooth or eye, the slave goes free. That is a קנס, a fixed penalty, and it is not paid based on one's own admission. So even the truth would not have cost the master anything without witnesses, and his oath did not deny money.

keyTerms.meaning: A fixed penalty set by the תורה, not regular repayment of damage

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix this up with step 22. Both are injuries, but a free person gets payment for damage, while the slave going free is a קנס. That difference decides liable or exempt.

phrases.english: His slave said to him:
"You knocked out my tooth
and you blinded my eye,"
phrases.notes: These are the injuries for which a slave goes free from his master.

phrases.english: and he says: "I did not knock it out and I did not blind it";
"I make you swear," and he said "Amen": he is exempt.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לוֹ עַבְדּוֹ: ״הִפַּלְתָּ אֶת שִׁינִּי וְסִימִּיתָ אֶת עֵינִי״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The contrasting case to step 22: an injury that leads to a קנס rather than a regular payment.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Denying under oath that you knocked out your slave's tooth or eye leaves you exempt, because the slave's freedom is a קנס and not paid based on your own admission.

steps.title: The general rule: paying based on your own admission
steps.stepSummary: Anyone who would pay based on his own admission is liable for a false oath. Anyone who would not pay based on his own admission is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is the rule: whoever pays based on his own word is liable, and whoever does not pay based on his own word is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה sums up all its cases with one general rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The test is simple: if the man had admitted the truth, would he have had to pay? If yes, his false oath denied money and he is liable. If no, as with any קנס, his oath did not deny money and he is exempt.
steps.whatToRemember: The key question for שבועת הפקדון is whether his own admission would have made him pay. If yes, he is liable (injury, theft, an ox killing an ox). If no, he is exempt (קנס cases such as rape, seduction, killing a slave, or knocking out a slave's tooth or eye).
steps.whyThisMatters: This one rule explains every liable and exempt case in the משנה, so the learner does not need to memorize each case separately.

phrases.english: This is the rule:

phrases.aramaic: כׇּל הַמְשַׁלֵּם עַל פִּי עַצְמוֹ – חַיָּיב,
phrases.english: anyone who pays based on his own admission is liable,

phrases.aramaic: וְשֶׁאֵינוֹ מְשַׁלֵּם עַל פִּי עַצְמוֹ – פָּטוּר.
phrases.english: and one who does not pay based on his own admission is exempt.
phrases.notes: He means cases where only witnesses can make him pay, like a קנס.

steps.triggerLanguage: זֶה הַכְּלָל: כׇּל הַמְשַׁלֵּם עַל פִּי עַצְמוֹ – חַיָּיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns all the paired cases before it into one general principle.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: A false oath denying money brings liability only if the person would have paid based on his own admission; claims that are a קנס bring no liability.

steps.title: Three students learning in רבה's study hall meet רב כהנא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins with a story: three students were learning מסכת שבועות in רבה's study hall, and רב כהנא met them and started to speak.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אחא בר הונא, רב שמואל son of רבה בר בר חנה, and רב יצחק son of רב יהודה learned שבועות in the house of רבה. רב כהנא met them and said...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up its next move. It introduces three students and רב כהנא, who is about to ask them a question about the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Nothing has been asked or ruled yet. This line only gives the setting and the people. The word 'said' at the end leads straight into רב כהנא's question in the next section.

keyTerms.meaning: The discussion that explains the משנה
He met them, came across them

phrases.english: GEMARA: Rav Aḥa bar Huna

phrases.aramaic: וְרַב שְׁמוּאֵל בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַבָּה בַּר בַּר חָנָה
phrases.english: and Rav Shmuel, son of Rabba bar bar Ḥana,
and Rav Yitzḥak, son of Rav Yehuda,
studied Shevuot in the study hall of Rabba.
phrases.notes: "Shevuot" here is the name of this מסכת, the one we are learning.

phrases.english: Rav Kahana met them and said

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב אַחָא בַּר הוּנָא וְרַב שְׁמוּאֵל בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַבָּה בַּר בַּר חָנָה וְרַב יִצְחָק בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב יְהוּדָה, תְּנוֹ שְׁבוּעוֹת בֵּי רַבָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts the גמרא's discussion of the משנה with a story that leads into רב כהנא's question.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: No ruling yet. This sets the scene for רב כהנא's question about the משנה.
